title: Janmashtami: the girl in the cell
hook: the baby girl left in Kamsa's cell rises as the Goddess: the Lord's hidden power, revealed
carry: yogamaya: god hides in plain sight

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rakhi and its promise of protection. Today, back to the prison on Janmashtami night, and the baby girl left in the cell.

Midnight in King Kamsa's prison. Krishna is born, the guards asleep, the chains loose, and Vasudeva carries the baby through the storm and across the Yamuna to the cowherd village. In Yashoda's house he leaves his son, picks up her newborn daughter, and carries her back through the rain. By morning he's in his cell again, chains on, as if nothing happened. The guards wake to the sound of a baby crying. They run to tell the king. And Kamsa comes down the stairs to the prison, for the eighth child.
screen: `THE SWAP IN THE NIGHT.` → `A BABY CRYING IN THE CELL.` → `KAMSA COMES DOWN THE STAIRS.`

segments.voice: Devaki begs him. It's a girl, she says. How could a little girl harm you? Let me keep just this one. Kamsa doesn't listen. The Bhagavata Purana says he seizes the baby by the feet and swings her to dash her against a stone. She slips out of his hands. She rises into the air, and in the sky she's no longer a baby. She's the Goddess, shining, with eight arms and weapons in every hand: Yogamaya, the power of the Lord's own mystery. It was her power, the Bhagavata says, that put the guards to sleep, and she had been born as Yashoda's daughter to make the whole rescue possible. She speaks to Kamsa from the sky: the one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Then she's gone. Now the teaching inside this night. Yogamaya is God's power to hide, and to work while hidden. Krishna himself later says he isn't revealed to everyone, because he's veiled by his yogamaya. Look at how God arrives here. Not with thunder. Carried through the rain in a basket, raised as a cowherd's boy, while the Goddess lies in a prison cell disguised as a baby girl nobody wanted. Many Hindus take this to heart: God often works hidden, through ordinary people and ordinary things, and the one everyone overlooks may be the holiest one in the room. It's part of why, at midnight, many families rock a little cradle with baby Krishna in it. The Lord of the universe, small enough to hold. Yogamaya: God hides in plain sight.
screen: `SHE SLIPS OUT OF HIS HANDS.` · `YOGAMAYA, THE GODDESS, IN THE SKY.` · `GOD WORKS HIDDEN.` · `A CRADLE AT MIDNIGHT.` · then, large: `YOGAMAYA: GOD HIDES IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you pray, picture the little cradle at midnight, or rock one if your family keeps it, and say softly, Jai Shri Krishna. Stay a moment with God made small enough to hold. If you don't pray, think of someone you usually overlook, at home, at school, at work, and wonder, just for a minute, what you haven't seen in them. Sit with that, and wait in the dark.
Janmashtami. The birth on the eighth night, and a rescue worked in secret by the Lord's own mystery.
Your line: yogamaya: god hides in plain sight. Even in a baby girl in a prison cell. Ninety-two days, and counting.

howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, then celebrate Krishna's birth with songs and by rocking a small cradle with an image of baby Krishna; the next day, especially in Maharashtra, teams form human pyramids to break a high-hung pot of curd, called dahi handi.

Janmashtami.meaning: the festival of Krishna's birth, on the eighth night

Kamsa.meaning: the cruel king who imprisoned Krishna's parents

Devaki.meaning: Krishna's birth mother, who could not keep him

Yashoda.meaning: the cowherd mother who raised Krishna

Yogamaya.meaning: the Goddess, the Lord's own mystery, born as Yashoda's daughter

Bhagavata Purana.meaning: an old book of stories about Vishnu and Krishna

recall: a thread tied as a promise of care

notes: Bhagavata 10.4: Devaki pleads that the child is a girl; Kamsa seizes her by the feet to dash her on a stone; she rises as the eight-armed Goddess and tells him his slayer is born elsewhere. Confirm details.
Yogamaya glossed as 'the power of the Lord's own mystery'. Confirm.
'Who never knew she had a daughter at all': Bhagavata 10.3 says Yashoda did not know the sex of her child due to Yogamaya's influence. Confirm.
Dahi handi on the day after Janmashtami (Gokulashtami) in Maharashtra. Confirm.
